guide.title: Exploring one-variable data and collecting data: review guide
guide.intro: This unit is about describing a single variable and about how data are collected, which decides what conclusions are allowed.

sections.title: Variables and categorical data
body: A categorical variable puts individuals into groups (eye colour, zip code). A quantitative variable is a number you can sensibly average (height, time). Summarise categorical data with counts or relative frequencies (count ÷ total), shown in bar charts or pie charts.
points: Numbers that are labels (zip codes, jersey numbers) are categorical.

sections.title: Describing quantitative data
body: Describe a distribution with shape, center, spread, and unusual values, in context. Use dotplots, histograms, stemplots, or boxplots.
points: Skewed right: mean is usually greater than the median. Skewed left: mean is usually less than the median.
The median and IQR are resistant to outliers. The mean, standard deviation, and range are not.
Outlier rule: below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR.

sections.title: Sampling and experiments
body: An observational study measures without intervening. An experiment imposes treatments. Only a well-designed experiment with random assignment supports cause-and-effect conclusions. Only random sampling supports generalising to the population.
points: Simple random sample: every group of n individuals is equally likely.
Stratified: split into similar groups (strata) and take a random sample from each.
Cluster: split into groups, randomly pick whole groups.
Bias: voluntary response, undercoverage, nonresponse, and wording all push results one way.
Experiment principles: comparison, random assignment, control of other variables, replication. Blocking groups similar units before assigning treatments within each block.

example.prompt: A random sample of 200 students at a school was asked how many hours they sleep. Can the results be generalised? Can they show that sleep causes better grades?
example.solution: Yes to the first: random sampling lets you generalise to all students at that school. No to the second: this is an observational study, so it cannot show cause and effect.

misconceptions: A biased method gives biased results however large the sample is.
“Random sampling and random assignment are the same.”
Sampling decides who is studied (generalising). Assignment decides who gets which treatment (cause and effect).
“Skewed right means most values are on the right.”
The long tail is on the right. Most values are on the left.

questions.prompt: Which of these variables is categorical?
choices: The zip code of a student's home
A student's number of siblings
The time a student takes to run a mile
A student's height in centimetres
questions.explanation: A zip code is a label that places students into groups. Its digits are not quantities, so averaging zip codes makes no sense.
choiceExplanations: Number of siblings is a count, which is quantitative.
Time is a measured quantity, so it is quantitative.
Height is a measured quantity, so it is quantitative.

questions.prompt: In a survey of 80 students, 20 said basketball is their favourite sport. What is the relative frequency of basketball?
questions.explanation: Relative frequency is the count divided by the total: 20/80 = 0.25.
choiceExplanations: 0.20 divides by 100 instead of by the total of 80.
60 is the number of students who did not choose basketball.
20 is the count (frequency), not the relative frequency.

questions.prompt: Researchers randomly assign 60 volunteers to sleep either 6 or 8 hours and then measure their reaction times. What kind of study is this?
choices: A sample survey
An observational study
An experiment
A census
questions.explanation: The researchers impose a treatment (amount of sleep) and randomly assign it, so this is an experiment.
choiceExplanations: A survey asks questions without assigning treatments.
An observational study does not impose treatments. Here the sleep amount is assigned.
A census measures every member of a population. Here 60 volunteers are studied.

questions.prompt: A distribution of household incomes is strongly skewed to the right. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: The mean and median are equal
The mean is greater than the median
The IQR is greater than the range
The median is greater than the mean
questions.explanation: A few very large incomes pull the mean toward the long right tail. The median is resistant, so it stays lower.
choiceExplanations: The mean and median are close only for roughly symmetric distributions.
The IQR covers the middle half of the data, so it can never be larger than the range.
That pattern goes with a left-skewed distribution.

questions.prompt: A data set has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which value is an outlier?
questions.explanation: IQR = 10, so the fences are 20 − 15 = 5 and 30 + 15 = 45. Only 48 is beyond a fence.
choiceExplanations: 35 is well inside both fences.
42 is below the upper fence of 45.
8 is above the lower fence of 5.

questions.prompt: A school lists its students by grade and randomly selects 25 students from each grade. What kind of sample is this?
choices: A convenience sample
A simple random sample
A cluster sample
A stratified random sample
questions.explanation: The population is split into groups (grades), and a random sample is taken from every group. That is stratified sampling.
choiceExplanations: The students are chosen at random, not because they are easy to reach.
In a simple random sample every group of students is equally likely. Here each grade is guaranteed exactly 25.
A cluster sample would randomly choose whole groups, such as entire homerooms, and survey everyone in them.

questions.prompt: Researchers compare two fertilizers using 20 plots: 10 in a sunny field and 10 in a shady field. Which design is best?
choices: Let the farmer choose which plots get each fertilizer
Randomly assign all 20 plots without regard to field
Within each field, randomly assign 5 plots to each fertilizer
Use fertilizer A in the sunny field and fertilizer B in the shady field
questions.explanation: Sunlight affects growth, so block by field and randomly assign treatments within each block. That separates the fertilizer effect from the sunlight effect.
choiceExplanations: Choices made by a person can introduce bias. Treatments should be randomly assigned.
This is random but ignores a known source of variation. Blocking by field gives a more precise comparison.
This confounds fertilizer with sunlight. A difference could be due to either.

questions.prompt: The data set 2, 4, 5, 9, 20 has mean 8 and median 5. If the value 20 is removed, what happens?
choices: The mean decreases by 3 and the median does not change
The mean decreases by 3 and the median decreases by 0.5
Both the mean and the median decrease by 3
The median decreases by 3 and the mean decreases by 0.5
questions.explanation: The remaining values 2, 4, 5, 9 have mean 20/4 = 5 and median (4 + 5)/2 = 4.5. The mean drops by 3, the median by only 0.5.
choiceExplanations: With four values left, the median becomes the average of the middle two, 4.5, so it does change.
The median is resistant to the extreme value, so it drops much less than the mean.
This swaps the two changes. The mean is the measure pulled by the outlier.
